pageIntro: Bloktopia is a crypto-focused metaverse set inside a virtual skyscraper of 21 floors, a nod to Bitcoin's 21 million coin supply. It was built as a place where people could learn about crypto, meet up, play games and own virtual real estate. & At Bloktopia, one of my main responsibilities was building Blok Arcade, a hub of hyper casual games for the metaverse with networking handled through Photon Fusion. & Two of the three launch titles started life as Unity Asset Store bundles that I took apart and rebuilt to fit Bloktopia's world. I designed and built the third, Crypto Rush, from scratch. & Across all three, the networking was the real engineering challenge. I built a custom synchronisation pattern for the arcade that kept traffic low and let players near a game watch scores and progress update in real time.
title: Bull Run
Crypto Connect (Hex Game)
Crypto Rush
introText: Bull Run started as a Unity Asset Store downhill ride template. I took it apart, kept what was worth keeping and rebuilt the rest to fit what the arcade needed. On a project like this, deciding what to keep and what to throw out is half the work. & To see the original template, [LINK] https://assetstore.unity.com/packages/templates/packs/downhill-ride-game-template-232870

Crypto Connect is a tile based puzzle game where players link tiles with their mouse to score points. It also started life as a Unity Asset Store bundle, but the brief was different this time. I had to strip it down and run it as a single player game in its own scene inside the metaverse, with no networking. & To see the original template, [LINK] https://assetstore.unity.com/packages/templates/packs/connect-game-template-232880

Crypto Rush is the one I owned from start to finish, covering the design, gameplay and networking. The brief was open, so the build was mine to shape. & The video shows the game from two angles: the player mid run, and an observer watching live from somewhere else in the metaverse. That second view is the spectator networking at work.
infoText: The original template gave me the basic structure. I rebuilt the player characters, the scoring system and the core gameplay loop from scratch to fit the arcade's style. & Like the rest of the arcade, Bull Run uses the custom Photon Fusion spectator networking, so nearby players can watch each other's scores update live.

The challenge on this one was the integration. I condensed the bundle's gameplay into a single scene and dropped it into Bloktopia without breaking the world around it. I added custom save and load, and reskinned the whole thing in the Bloktopia art direction so it didn't feel like a bolted on asset. & The gameplay loop is simple but well tuned. Linking tiles scores points, and linked tiles upgrade into higher value pieces that are harder to match but pay more. The game ends when no valid connections remain.

The game is a coin sorting loop against the clock. A randomised stream of Bitcoin and Ethereum coins comes in, and you sort Bitcoin to the left and Ethereum to the right, getting through as many as you can before the timer runs out. It's quick and simple, which is the hyper casual feel the arcade needed. & Crypto Rush pushed the spectator layer furthest, because spectators see every coin being sorted live. The synchronisation only sends what has changed, so network traffic stays low even when several spectators are watching at once.

pageIntro: Blokbuster is a fast multiplayer trivia game built for crowds, with up to 800 players in a single session. Each round asks a multiple choice question, and players race to the zone that matches their answer before the timer runs out. Pick the wrong zone and you're out. Pick the right one and you go through to the next round. & Rounds continue until either the questions or the players run out, and whoever is still standing at the end wins.
title: Blokbuster
infoText: Off the shelf networking can't run 800 concurrent players in one session on its own, so the game uses a hybrid setup. Photon Fusion handles the real time gameplay layer, which covers round progression, player movement and sending data from the host to clients. Azure SignalR handles the wider state synchronisation that keeps every player in agreement about what the world looks like. & When a player updates their state locally, the change goes through SignalR to the host, the host reconciles it, and the updated state goes back out to everyone connected. The two layers do different jobs at different scales, and most of the engineering went into getting them to work together cleanly. Match results and session data are saved to Azure Blob Storage at the end of each round. & I built the front end integration for both networking layers. That covered the SignalR client that sends and receives state on the Unity side, the Photon Fusion networking for the gameplay in the arena, and the trivia arena itself. Splitting the work like this is what lets it handle a load that a single networking layer couldn't.

pageIntro: Bionic Blitz was my first game, and the project that taught me what game development really involves. In 2017 a friend and I set up Topbox Studio with no studio experience between us. He did the graphics, I did the programming and animation setup, and we worked out the rest as we went. & It's a fast arcade game built for PC and Android. You play as OddBot, a mischievous robot draining power from enemies while dodging or disabling the ones that chase you on sight. It has unlockable power-ups, online leaderboards, multilingual support, and enemies that get harder as you go, each with its own behaviour and attack pattern.
title: Bionic Blitz
infoText: I wrote every line of code in Bionic Blitz, including the player controls, enemy AI, power-ups, scoring, localisation, leaderboards and the AdMob integration on the Android build. I also did all the animation setup in Unity. It shipped on Steam and Android. & I'll be honest about this codebase. It's the work of someone who didn't understand architecture yet. The systems are tangled, the patterns are inconsistent, and I'd build it very differently now. I'm including it anyway because what it taught me is worth more than a clean codebase would have been. Finishing it took over a year of nights and weekends with no template to copy, nobody more senior to ask and, since this was 2017, no AI to lean on. Every problem got solved the hard way, through documentation, forums and a lot of hours on Stack Overflow at 2am hoping someone had already hit the same wall. I wouldn't be building things the way I do now if I hadn't stuck with Bionic Blitz to the end. & What it taught me about architecture and scope, and about writing code that lasts, has shaped every project I've worked on since.

pageIntro: The Chicken and the Fox was meant to be the first in a series of multilingual children's books from Taylor's Tales, the company of children's author Randol Taylor, made in collaboration with Topbox Studio. In the end we only released one book, but the system we built for it was designed to handle many. & The book mixes educational elements into the story, so young readers have things to interact with as well as read. Each page has its own interactables and facts to find. & The app is split into two Unity projects, and that split is the heart of the engineering. The main project reads and presents books. The uploader, which I designed and built from scratch, handles all the content creation, so the art, page layouts, audio, paragraphs and page metadata all live there. The main project never touches raw assets and only ever reads finished asset bundles. Keeping them separate meant the main app stayed small, and the content pipeline could handle as many books as we wanted to ship.
title: Taylor's Tales
Taylor's Tales Uploader
introText: The main project is the app the reader opens. It loads the asset bundles for whichever book the user picks and builds the pages on the fly from what's inside them. & The video shows a short walkthrough of the book, which has 25 pages, each with its own facts and interactables. It was built for Android and iOS.

The uploader is the content side of Taylor's Tales, and it was entirely my design. It's a separate Unity project built around a set of custom editor windows, and each one handles a specific part of putting a page of the book together, from writing the text to packaging the artwork and the facts readers discover along the way. & Everything it produces is either an asset bundle or a JSON file, and that's all the main app ever reads. Writers and artists work in the uploader, and the main app stays lean. The tools support English, Irish, French and Spanish, though only English and Irish have been written so far. The video shows the process of creating the first two pages of The Chicken and the Fox.
infoText: The main app is deliberately thin. On startup it reads the JSON manifest for the selected book, pulls the matching asset bundles from persistent data and builds each page at runtime, with the layout, art, audio, text and interactables all coming from the bundle. There's no book specific code in the main project. Adding a new title means dropping in a new set of bundles and a manifest, without rebuilding or redeploying the app. & Support for multiple languages runs off the same system. Each page's paragraphs are stored in the JSON metadata by language, so switching language is a manifest lookup rather than a content swap. The whole app is built for Android and iOS from a single Unity codebase.

The first section covers the page text. The book's source text is kept in one JSON file per language, and for now that means English and Irish. In the Page Text window I choose the page and the language, and one button pulls that page's paragraphs out of the source file and into the window, where they can be checked and edited against a live preview. The preview also highlights the page's trigger words, which are the words that link to facts later in the pipeline. Saving writes them into the book's page data JSON, which holds the text for every page in each language and is what the main app reads to fill in each paragraph. The video does this for English and then for Irish, and shows the JSON file filling in after each save. & The second section builds the page itself. Each page is its own scene, with an environment canvas holding the artwork and an interaction canvas holding the things readers can touch. With page 1 open, the Environment window checks the scene for both canvases and a skybox, and only allows the build once it finds them. The build saves the canvases as prefabs and packs them with the skybox into a single asset bundle for that page. During development the bundles were written to persistent data, and at release they were served from Azure Blob Storage. The video builds page 1 and then repeats the process for page 2. & The third section handles the facts. Every trigger word marked in the book's text has a fact behind it, along with a folder of images in the project. The Facts window reads the fact data from JSON and lists every fact, showing its trigger word in each language, the information that goes with it and thumbnails of the images readers will see. In the video I expand them all so everything is visible, show that the output folder is empty and then upload. Each fact's images are packed into their own asset bundle, and a Facts.json file is written that links every fact to its bundle, so the main app knows exactly which bundle to load for each word. The video finishes by showing the output folder again, now filled with the new bundles. & The last section shows the book's word library, which lists every unique word in the book for the selected language, each of which needs its own audio clip. This worked out much better than having someone read straight from the book. The narrator simply reads through the list, and we cut the recording into a separate clip for each word. The sentence library works the same way, listing every page's text in reading order so the full sentences can be recorded and split in one session.

pageIntro: I was the fourth person hired at Coach Cube, an AI fitness hardware startup of seven people, and I’ve been the lead front end developer since day one. In a team this size, being the lead also means being the only one, and doing whatever else the day needs. I was part of the early technical conversations. We debated the stack, built prototypes, and threw things out and started again until we landed on the right technologies. The front end has been mine from start to finish. & In my first week I started teaching myself solutions architecture so I could contribute properly to those decisions, and I’ve kept at it since. Knowing why a stack is shaped the way it is has made me a better engineer at every layer, including the ones I don’t work in day to day.
title: Coach Cube
introText: Lead front end developer at an AI fitness hardware startup, building the Unity 6 client, its real time data layer and the embedded React UI.
infoText: The Coach Cube front end is a Unity 6 app on URP. It uses Zenject for dependency injection and a message broker pattern, so tracking, AI, hardware and UI never talk to each other directly and can each be tested on their own. Every system has its own assembly with explicit dependencies, which has kept the codebase clean as it’s grown. & The hardest problem has been the real time data layer. The client gets pose tracking data and workout events from the backend over Redis, using two of its features. Pub/Sub carries rep progress, which updates constantly, so losing the odd message doesn’t matter. Streams carry rep counts, which have to arrive. There’s also a WebSocket connection to the Vitruvian resistance hardware. Redis was new to me when I joined. I learned it from scratch, ran it locally in Docker and wired it into Unity through Zenject, so the rest of the codebase never has to know it’s there. & UniTask handles async throughout. ElevenLabs TTS gives the AI coach its voice, and a local cache keeps latency and costs down. The whole UI is a React app running inside an embedded Chromium browser. I chose that over Unity’s built in UI because it’s faster to iterate on and much nicer to work with, and I built that integration myself. & Outside Unity, I built and own an internal Vue 3 web app with Vite, Tailwind and Firebase. Our trainers use it to build workout templates and run sessions. It calls our Spring Boot backend over REST, which then streams the workout into Redis for the Unity client to pick up. I didn’t write the backend, but I worked closely on its design, especially the Redis event contracts.
additionalText: My role also grew into product ownership. I owned the graphics pipeline and worked with our contract designers to get assets delivered. I also owned the internal web app that sends data between our backend and the Unity client. Neither of those is normally part of a front end role. I took them on because someone had to. & I also took the reins on marketing. I filmed many of our promotional videos for Instagram and featured in a lot of them myself, and you can watch some of them in the My Claim to Fame section of this page. & A startup at this stage doesn’t let you stay in your lane. If something needs to exist and nobody else is going to build it, you learn what you need and ship it. I love that pace. The part I’m proudest of is the detail, the small interactions and the polish that take ten times longer than the feature itself. & As we got closer to launch I moved into a Technical Account Manager role alongside development. I supported 30 to 40 live demos for investors and clients. I deployed the full stack on site, including the Docker services, the connection between the dashboard and the backend, and the Redis messaging. I also helped install and test the physical prototype, which went on to run around 300 user sessions. When something broke on a live unit I was the one who went to site, read the container logs and got it running again before the next demo. & From July 2026 I co-managed our first commercial partnership, a 16 week pilot with a premium workspace operator. I was a regular point of contact for their team and the link between them and our engineers. Watching real users struggle with something I built has made me a better developer.

pageIntro: RightScan is a mobile app that tells you whether a food product is vegan, vegetarian or halal. You scan the barcode and get a clear verdict for each diet, with the reason and the ingredient responsible. & It's strict by default. If the app isn't sure, it shows a warning rather than a green tick, because a wrong yes is worse than a cautious maybe. Diet preferences stay on the phone, and the app stores no names, emails or locations. It's currently in an Android beta that I'm testing in shops.
title: RightScan
introText: Scan a food barcode and get a vegan, vegetarian and halal verdict with the reason behind it.
additionalText: RightScan is the most ambitious thing I've built with Claude Code, and the workflow is as much the project as the app. Before any code was written I wrote planning documents covering requirements, architecture, data model, API contracts and a roadmap split into phases and numbered tasks, each with its own "done when" test. Those documents are the source of truth over the code. & CLAUDE.md works as an operating manual for the agents. Each session starts by reading a short status file and a knowledge graph of the codebase, then only the docs its task points to. It ends with tests and CI green, the status file updated and one pull request on its own branch. In autopilot mode the agents work through the roadmap and merge their own pull requests once CI passes, stopping for anything that changes a verdict, costs money or fails twice. Agents even drive my test phone over USB to check the app on a real device, with strict rules about confirming which app is on screen before every input. & My role is product owner and architect. I set the rules, review the decisions, and do the real world testing with the beta on my phone. Every architecture decision is logged and numbered, and there are well over a hundred of them.
infoText: The app is React Native with Expo and TypeScript. It makes one HTTPS call per scan, and the backend owns all the verdict logic, so rules can change without shipping a new app. Barcode scanning runs on the device, with check digit validation and two frame confirmation so a misread never reaches the server. & The backend is ASP.NET Core on .NET 10, running on Azure Container Apps with Azure SQL. It looks products up in Open Food Facts and its sister databases in parallel, with timeouts and caching, and translates foreign language ingredient lists through Azure Translator, caching every translation. & The verdict engine is pluggable. Vegan and vegetarian rules are declared in data, while halal has its own six step rule set. Rules match canonical ingredient IDs such as E471 rather than raw text, and every verdict carries reason codes and a ruleset version. Around 800 backend tests run against recorded real products, so CI never calls a live service. Every green build on main deploys to Azure automatically, and app updates ship over the air.

pageIntro: Every year my friends and I run a Premier League sweepstake. Before the season starts, each of us picks three players to score and three to assist. Every player has Golden Boot odds (Isak was 8/1, for example), and your three picks' odds have to add up to at least 125/1. The same rule applies to assists. That stops everyone piling onto Haaland and makes the picks interesting. & Every season I build a website we all use to follow the race. This year it's a live leaderboard for 17 of us, with goals on one side and assists on the other, updated automatically all season.
title: PL Sweepstake
introText: A live goals and assists leaderboard for a season long Premier League sweepstake with friends.
additionalText: This year's version was built with Claude Code. Before any code was written I wrote two documents: a CLAUDE.md describing the architecture, data rules and constraints, and a build brief splitting the work into phases, from scaffolding through to a final verification phase. Claude Code built it phase by phase, and I reviewed and tested each phase before moving on to the next. & My job was the decisions. I tested the data sources before picking one, and dropped the Fantasy Premier League API because its assists aren't the official numbers. When something didn't behave the way the docs said, I measured it and wrote the finding into CLAUDE.md, so every session started from the same facts.
infoText: The site is a Blazor WebAssembly app on .NET 10, hosted on GitHub Pages. There's no server and no database. The browser only ever reads a stats file that ships with the site. & A small .NET console tool builds that file. It pulls per match goals and assists from ESPN and adds them up itself, because ESPN's season totals lag hours behind. Matches are cached as recent, unsettled or settled, so late stat corrections still get picked up and finished matches are never fetched again. Players are matched by ESPN ID, never by name. ESPN's data has two players named Igor Jesus and ten named Bruno Fernandes. & GitHub Actions runs the fetcher on a schedule and redeploys when the numbers change. GitHub's 15 minute schedule turned out to fire roughly every 49 minutes, so on match days a separate workflow checks every 5 minutes through the likely match windows. 86 tests cover the leaderboard maths, the ESPN parsing and a check that every pick maps to a real player, and they all run before every deploy.

pageIntro: LifeBot is a tool I built for myself to stay organised. I hold the power button on my phone, say whatever I need to do, and it lands in the right to do list. It works from the lock screen, so there's no unlocking, opening an app or typing. & It keeps several lists and works out which one each item belongs in from what I said. If I start with the word calendar, it creates a calendar event instead, reading the day, time and length from the sentence.
title: LifeBot
introText: A voice controlled Android tool that turns anything I say into a to do item or a calendar event.
additionalText: I'm a Unity and C# developer and had never written Kotlin or an Android app before this. I built it with Claude Code, set up as a mentor rather than a code generator. My CLAUDE.md asked it to explain Android concepts through Unity ones, so an Activity was a Scene and a StateFlow was a UnityEvent, and to explain the why behind every decision. & The work was split into milestones, and each one had to build, install and pass a test on my phone before the next one started. A handoff document recorded what the phone actually did in each session, the decisions made along the way and what was still open, so every new session picked up exactly where the last one stopped. I built the whole thing from VS Code and the terminal, without Android Studio.
infoText: LifeBot registers itself as the phone's digital assistant, which is what lets a long press of the power button open it over the lock screen. It listens continuously, restarts the speech recognizer after every pause and joins the pieces together until I tap stop. It prefers Android's on device recognizer, so nothing I say leaves the phone, and the app doesn't even have internet permission. & The parsing is plain Kotlin with no Android code in it, so it can be unit tested on a PC. The command parser accepts loose phrasing and fuzzy matches list names, so small recognition mistakes still find the right list. A list guesser scores each item against the words already in each list and only files it when there's a clear winner. Anything it can't place goes to Miscellaneous. An event parser reads the day, time and duration for calendar entries. The three parsers are covered by 82 unit tests. & Some of the most useful work was finding out what Android won't allow. The assistant session never receives key events, so releasing the power button to stop recording is impossible. To qualify as an assistant the app also has to declare its own stub speech recognizer, so it has to pick the real one explicitly. Each finding went into the project docs so it was never relearned.
